passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4. Elizabeth Miss, Wednesday.
Observation: Today we rearranged seats so everyone sits with someone new. Thomas refused to move from his window seat. "I always sit here," he said, gripping the desk. His new seat, beside Anjali near the fan, is just as good; last week he told me he wished he could sit near the fan. When I asked what worried him, he said, "I don't know. It's just not my place." He also brings the same lunch every day and takes the same staircase even when the other one is closer.
What I did: I agreed he could try the new seat for two days only, and we'll talk again on Friday. He moved, slowly.

qa.q: Where is Thomas's new seat?
qa.a: His new seat is beside Anjali near the fan.

qa.q: Why did Thomas grip the desk when asked to move?
qa.a: Thomas felt anxious, because the window seat is what he knows and changing felt risky to him. He felt that way even though the new seat was just as good, maybe better.

qa.q: Why was the two-day trial a good idea?
qa.a: It made the change small and safe, with a promise to talk again, so Thomas could test the new seat without feeling he had lost his place for good.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Thomas slowly moves beside her?
qa.a: Anjali may feel a little unsure at first, wondering if he minds sitting there, and may try to make him feel welcome.

grounding: Shows a boy insisting on the same seat, lunch and staircase because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage:
Wednesday
Today Amma made poha instead of upma. I didn't eat it. I always have upma. Irawati ate mine too and said the poha was really nice, with peanuts. Amma said I can't have the same thing every single day of my life. Why not? I like knowing what's coming. Then Papa said we'd take the new road to school because the old one has digging. I cried a bit. The new road had a big tree with parrots, but I didn't look at it much. Tomorrow I want upma, the old road and my same seat. Amma calls me her little upma boy. I don't mind.
Gautam

qa.q: What did Amma make instead of upma?
qa.a: Amma made poha instead of upma.

qa.q: Why did Gautam cry a bit about the new road?
qa.a: He likes knowing what's coming, so a change of route felt risky and upsetting even though the new road had a tree with parrots.

qa.q: How could Amma help Gautam try new things?
qa.a: She could make small changes one at a time, like poha once a week with upma on other days, and talk about something nice on the new road before they go.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel about eating the poha?
qa.a: Irawati clearly enjoyed the poha with peanuts and may not understand why the change upset Gautam so much.

grounding: Shows a boy insisting on the same breakfast, route and seat because change feels riskier than what he knows.

passage: In their village near Nashik, a new footbridge had opened across the stream, cutting the walk to school by ten minutes. Salma started using it on the first day. Kiran, nine, kept taking the long path around the field, the one he had walked since class one. "Come on, the bridge is quicker," Salma called from the other side. "I like my way," Kiran said. "I know every stone." In the monsoon the long path turned to mud, and he arrived at school with muddy legs, late twice. Even so, when Salma dared him to try the bridge, he shook his head. "What if it's not as good?"

qa.q: How much time did the new footbridge cut from the walk?
qa.a: The footbridge cut the walk to school by ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Kiran's "What if it's not as good?" reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that Kiran feels uneasy about trying something new, so changing feels riskier to him than staying with what he knows, even after the mud and being late twice.

qa.q: What small step could Salma suggest?
qa.a: Salma could suggest trying the bridge just once, walking it together, and going back to the old path the next day if he doesn't like it.

qa.q: How might Salma feel calling from the other side of the bridge?
qa.a: Salma may feel puzzled and a little impatient, but keeps inviting Kiran, which shows real care.

grounding: Shows a boy keeping to his usual long route even when a better one exists, because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage: Every Saturday in Durban, Sami, eight, went to the public library with his big sister Lindiwe, sat at the same corner table by the fish tank, and ate the same jam sandwich at noon. This week, things had moved. The fish tank was now near the windows, and a reading nook with beanbags filled the old corner. Sami froze in the doorway. "Where's my table?" "Look, beanbags!" Lindiwe said. "I want MY table." He sat stiffly at another desk, arms folded, not reading. At noon he refused a new sandwich from the café and ate his jam one. After a while, he crept over to the beanbags, just to look. He sat on one. "It's… okay," he said. Then, quieter, "It's actually squishy."

qa.q: Where had the fish tank been moved to?
qa.a: The fish tank was now near the windows.

qa.q: Why did Sami refuse to enjoy the new beanbags at first?
qa.a: His usual table and routine felt safe and known, so any change felt risky, even though the new nook was fine.

qa.q: What small step helped Sami try the change?
qa.a: He crept over to the beanbags just to look, and then sat on one. Trying a tiny piece of the change let him discover it was okay.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Sami says the beanbag is squishy?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and amused after his stubborn start, and glad he tried it on his own.

grounding: A boy insists on his usual library table and sandwich when things change, then slowly tries the new beanbags.

passage: At the school's summer camp, the dining hall had a new menu: dosa, poha, fruit, or aloo paratha. Manvir, nine, sat at his usual end of table three and asked for aloo paratha, like every day. His friend Rajni said, "Try the dosa, it's crispy." "No. Paratha." Camp teacher Jasleen ma'am noticed that Manvir also walked the long way to the pool, past the kitchen, though a new garden path was shorter. "Why that way?" she asked. He shrugged. "It's my way." On Friday, Rajni dared him to walk the garden path with her. He went slowly, looking around. Butterflies circled the hibiscus. "Hm," he said. "Same pool at the end." The next morning he tried half a dosa.

qa.q: Where was Manvir's usual seat?
qa.a: At the end of table three.

qa.q: Why did Manvir keep walking the long way to the pool?
qa.a: The usual way felt safe because he knew it, and trying the new path felt like a risk, even though it was shorter and fine.

qa.q: What helped Manvir try something new, and what could adults learn from it?
qa.a: Rajni's friendly dare to walk the garden path together. A small, shared first try made the change feel safe, which led him to taste half a dosa too.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when Manvir tries half a dosa?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased, as her patient invitations finally helped her friend try something new.

grounding: At summer camp, a boy sticks to the same seat, breakfast and route until a friend helps him try a new path.

passage: Every morning Vishal ate the same thing: two rotis with jaggery, never anything else. Then he walked to the village school by the same path, past the temple, the well and the broken tractor, always on the left side. One Monday the path by the well was muddy, and his cousin Vijay pointed to the new cement road. "This way is shorter. And dry." Vishal stopped. "No. We go by the well." "Why?" "Because that's the way." He walked through the mud, his chappals squelching, and arrived late. At lunch Vijay offered him a bite of poha. Vishal shook his head. "I only eat rotis." "You've never even tried it." Vishal looked at the poha for a long time before he pushed it back.

qa.q: What did Vishal eat every morning?
qa.a: Two rotis with jaggery.

qa.q: Why did Vishal walk through the mud instead of taking the dry road?
qa.a: He felt uneasy about changing, so the old muddy path felt safer than a new road, even though it made him late.

qa.q: What small step could help Vishal try something new?
qa.a: Walk the new road once with Vijay on a dry day, or taste just a spoon of poha, so change feels small and safe.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Vishal's habits?
qa.a: Vijay seems puzzled and a bit amused that Vishal chooses mud and rotis over a shorter road and a new taste.

grounding: A boy sticks to the same breakfast and the same path even when a dry, shorter road and new food are fine.

passage: On the first Monday of the new term in their Toronto school, Ms Clarke moved everyone's seats. Yosef found his name card by the window, next to Fatima, instead of at his old desk by the door. He stood beside the old desk with his backpack on. "I sit here." "This term you sit by the window," Ms Clarke said. "You'll like the view." "I like the door." He sat by the window only when she waited beside him. All morning he kept looking back at his old desk. At lunch Fatima showed him that you could see squirrels on the fence from the window. Yosef watched one run along the top, then quickly looked away, as if he wasn't allowed to enjoy it yet.

qa.q: Where was Yosef's new seat?
qa.a: By the window, next to Fatima.

qa.q: Why did Yosef keep looking back at his old desk?
qa.a: He felt unsettled and a little anxious, because the old seat by the door felt safe and familiar, and the new one felt risky even though it was fine.

qa.q: How could Ms Clarke help Yosef settle into the new seat?
qa.a: Give him a small job by the window, or agree to try it for a week and then talk, so the change feels less sudden.

qa.q: What is it like for Fatima to sit beside Yosef on the first day?
qa.a: Fatima seems friendly and patient, showing him the squirrels to help him like the new seat.

grounding: A boy resists a new seat by the window because his usual desk feels safer, even though the new place is fine.

passage: At the residential summer camp, the mess served something different each morning: dosa, upma, parathas. Pranav, eleven, took two slices of bread and jam every single day. He sat in the same corner chair, and he walked to the pool by the long path round the hall, even after the counsellor, Vidya ma'am, showed everyone the short cut through the garden. On Thursday his corner chair was taken. Pranav stood holding his tray until the boy moved. "Why do you always do the same thing?" the boy asked. Pranav shrugged. "It's fine. I know it's fine." That evening Vidya ma'am sat beside him at dinner. "Tomorrow, one new thing only," she said. "You choose which." Pranav thought for a long time. "Maybe the garden path."

qa.q: What did Pranav eat every morning at camp?
qa.a: Two slices of bread and jam.

qa.q: Why does Pranav keep doing the same things at camp?
qa.a: He feels safer with what he knows; trying new food or a new path feels risky, so the familiar choices feel fine even when better ones are there.

qa.q: Why is Vidya ma'am's one-new-thing idea a good one?
qa.a: It keeps the change small and lets Pranav choose, so trying something new feels less risky.

qa.q: How might the boy in the corner chair see Pranav's habits?
qa.a: The boy seems curious and a bit puzzled, asking why Pranav always does the same thing.

grounding: At camp, a boy keeps the same breakfast, seat and route even when alternatives are fine, until a counsellor suggests one small change.

passage:
Monday. Hemant, nine, sat in the same seat at the dining table as always and asked for the same breakfast: two idlis, no chutney. His older brother Farhan said, "Try the dosa, Mummy made it special." Hemant shook his head. "I like idli."

Wednesday. The road to school was being repaired, and Papa took a different lane. Hemant grew tense. "This isn't our road." "It's shorter," Farhan said. "It's wrong," Hemant muttered, gripping his bag.

Friday. The new lane passed a sweet shop and a park with swings. Farhan pointed at the swings. "See? It's nice." Hemant looked. The swings looked fun. But he still said, "I want the old road back." At breakfast the next day, he asked for two idlis, no chutney.

qa.q: What does Hemant always ask for at breakfast?
qa.a: Two idlis, no chutney.

qa.q: Why did Hemant grow tense on the new lane?
qa.a: Changing the route felt risky and uncomfortable, so the familiar road felt safer even though the new lane was fine.

qa.q: What small step could help Hemant with changes?
qa.a: His family could let him try one new thing at a time, like one bite of dosa or stopping at the swings, so change feels less scary.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Hemant's habits?
qa.a: Farhan seems patient but a little puzzled, pointing out the nice things about change.

grounding: It shows a child who insists on the same breakfast and route, as change feels riskier than what he knows, over several days.

passage: Deepak, you don't want to try the new school bus? Let me tell you about me at nine, a boy in Patna. I ate the same breakfast every day: poha with peanuts. I sat in the same corner at school. I walked the same road home, the long way past the pond, even though a shorter lane existed. One day my mother made upma. I refused and went to school hungry. I told myself poha was the best. Honestly, I'd never tried upma. Then one day my friend, a boy called Raju, dragged me down the short lane because it was raining. I was scared. But there was a sweet shop and a dog with puppies. I started going that way every day. Your Pankaj dadu learned that the usual isn't always the best. It's just the usual.

qa.q: What breakfast did Pankaj eat every day?
qa.a: Poha with peanuts.

qa.q: Why did young Pankaj refuse the upma?
qa.a: Trying something new felt risky, so the familiar poha felt safer, even though he had never tasted upma.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Pankaj try something new?
qa.a: When Raju dragged him down the short lane in the rain, he discovered it was better and started going that way.

qa.q: How might Pankaj's mother have felt when he left hungry?
qa.a: His mother probably felt worried and frustrated that he refused food over a small change.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, he insisted on the same breakfast and route because change felt riskier than the usual.

passage: On Muharram, a procession closed the main road in their Hyderabad neighbourhood, and Asif, eight, couldn't take his usual route to the park. His older sister Noor said, "We'll go the back way." Asif stopped. "No. I want the usual way." "It's closed, Asif." "Then I'm not going." He sat on the steps, arms folded. Noor waited. The back lane was fine, shady and quiet. Asif had never been down it. "It's the same park," Noor said. "It won't feel the same," he mumbled. Finally she held his hand and they walked slowly. He looked at every house suspiciously. At the park, he played on his usual swing. On the way back, he said, "The back lane was okay." But the next day, he wanted the old road again.

qa.q: Why was the main road closed?
qa.a: A Muharram procession closed it.

qa.q: Why did Asif refuse to take the back lane at first?
qa.a: Changing his route felt risky and uncomfortable, so he preferred not going at all to trying a new way.

qa.q: How did Noor help Asif try the new route?
qa.a: She waited patiently, held his hand, and walked slowly with him, making the change feel safer.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Asif wants the old road again?
qa.a: Noor might feel amused and a little tired, knowing change takes time for him.

grounding: It shows a child who insists on his usual route even when the alternative is fine, because change feels riskier than what he knows.

passage:
It was Navratri, and the whole family was going to the big garba ground. Dhruv refused to get into the car.

"I sit behind Papa. Always."

"Today Yogesh bhaiya is sitting there," said Mummy. "You sit by the window. You'll see the lights."

"No. Behind Papa."

At breakfast that morning, he had also refused the new poha and asked for plain toast, like every day. And he'd made them walk the long way to the temple, because it was the way he knew.

Yogesh bhaiya said, "Dhruv, the window seat is better tonight. The whole street has lights."

Dhruv sat stiffly by the window. For the first ten minutes, he stared straight ahead. Then a giant lit-up peacock passed, and he pressed his nose to the glass.

qa.q: Where did Dhruv always want to sit?
qa.a: Behind Papa.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv refuse the window seat, the new poha and the new route?
qa.a: Dhruv felt uneasy about change, because the usual seat, food and route felt safe and anything new felt risky.

qa.q: What helped Dhruv try the window seat?
qa.a: Yogesh bhaiya gave a reason to try it, the festival lights, and Dhruv was allowed to settle in slowly.

qa.q: How might Yogesh bhaiya feel when Dhruv pressed his nose to the glass?
qa.a: Yogesh bhaiya might feel pleased and amused that Dhruv enjoyed the window seat after all.

grounding: During a festival, a child insists on the same seat, breakfast and route, even when alternatives are fine.

passage:
"Manoj, it's Makar Sankranti. Try the til laddoo for breakfast."

"No, Jyoti didi. I want bread and jam."

"You have bread and jam every day."

"That's why I want it."

"And why won't you take the new bus route to school? It's shorter."

"The old route is the route."

"And your desk? Ma'am said you can move near the window."

"I like my desk."

"Manoj, why?"

He thought. "Because I know what happens. With new things, I don't know."

"But new things can be good too."

"Or bad."

Jyoti held out a small piece of laddoo. "Just one bite. If you hate it, bread and jam."

Manoj took the tiniest nibble. Chewed. "It's... okay."

"Only okay?"

"Maybe good. But tomorrow, bread and jam."

qa.q: What does Manoj have for breakfast every day?
qa.a: Bread and jam.

qa.q: Why does Manoj want to keep the same breakfast, route and desk?
qa.a: Manoj feels safer with the usual, because he knows what happens, and new things feel risky and uncertain.

qa.q: What did Jyoti didi do that helped Manoj try something new?
qa.a: Jyoti offered just one bite with a safe backup, so trying the laddoo felt small and low-risk.

qa.q: How does Jyoti didi seem to feel about Manoj's habits?
qa.a: Jyoti didi seems patient and gently amused, wanting Manoj to see that new things can be good too.

grounding: During a festival, a child sticks to the same breakfast, route and desk because change feels riskier than the familiar.

passage:
I'm Jeevan. Last summer holidays, we went to Nani's house for a month.

On the first day, Urmila didi wanted to take a new path to the market, past the pond. I said no. We had to go the road way, the one we always took.

At lunch Nani made a new dish, jackfruit curry. I only ate rice and dal. I always eat rice and dal.

Urmila didi said, "Why don't you try one new thing?" I didn't want to. New things felt scary.

On the fifth day, she took me the pond way anyway. There were ducks and a little bridge! I loved it.

After that, I tried the jackfruit curry too. It was nice. But now I know new things aren't always bad.

qa.q: What new dish did Nani make at lunch?
qa.a: Jackfruit curry.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan refuse the new path and the new dish at first?
qa.a: Jeevan felt scared of new things, because the usual path and food felt safe and anything different felt risky.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan try new things?
qa.a: Urmila didi took Jeevan the pond way, and discovering the ducks and bridge made trying the curry easier too.

qa.q: How might Urmila didi have felt when Jeevan loved the pond path?
qa.a: Urmila didi probably felt happy and relieved that Jeevan finally enjoyed something new.

grounding: A child on summer holidays insists on the usual route and food because change feels risky, until a new path surprises them.

passage:
Winter camp notes, Day 3, hill school near Shimla
Varun has again asked for the corner bunk nearest the door, though the heater is at the other end and the corner is freezing. At breakfast he wanted plain toast only; the aloo parathas smelled wonderful and he didn't try one. On today's walk he asked to take the same path as yesterday, not the new trail by the apple orchard, even when Ayesha said it was shorter and led to a frozen waterfall. "I know the old way," he said. I didn't push. I asked him to walk just the first stretch of the new trail with Ayesha and me, and promised we could turn back at the bend. He went past the bend. At the waterfall he smiled and asked if we could come again tomorrow.

qa.q: Which bunk does Varun keep asking for?
qa.a: The corner bunk nearest the door.

qa.q: Why does Varun keep choosing the old path and plain toast?
qa.a: What he already knows feels safe and predictable, so the new trail or the parathas make him uneasy, even when the change looks perfectly fine.

qa.q: Which step helped Varun try the new trail, and why did it work?
qa.a: Walking only the first stretch together, with a promise to turn back at the bend, because a small, safe try made the change feel less risky.

qa.q: How might Ayesha see Varun's choices?
qa.a: Ayesha may find it puzzling that Varun picks the colder, longer options, and is probably pleased when he reaches the waterfall and wants to come again.

grounding: Shows a child insisting on the same bunk, breakfast and route even when alternatives are fine, because change feels riskier than the familiar.
